name: Reactive Devaluation
description: A proposal can lose value in your eyes simply because it comes from an adversary or distrusted out-group. The source label poisons evaluation before the content gets a fair read.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to stakeholder negotiation, moderation appeals, dispute resolution, participatory design, civic products, and polarized communities. A sound proposal can be rejected because of who suggests it, not what it says.
prevalence_note: Known in negotiation, mediation, conflict, and polarization work, but only occasionally imported into product or organizational-design conversations.

findings.description: Across three studies in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict context, peace proposals were judged less favorably when attributed to the opposing side than when attributed to one's own side. Participants also construed source-labeled proposals as relatively worse for their own group and better for the adversary.
findings.source_title: Reactive Devaluation of an “Israeli” vs. “Palestinian” Peace Proposal

findings.description: Nine laboratory experiments (~450 subjects) testing psychological barriers to litigation settlement found that a settlement offer evaluated favorably in the abstract (or when proposed by an ally or neutral party) was more likely to be devalued when attributed to the litigation adversary -- reactive devaluation directly demonstrated in a legal-dispute-resolution context, alongside independently-tested framing and equity-seeking effects. A genuine, independent extension of the reactive-devaluation mechanism from the Israeli-Palestinian conflict context (the corpus's existing evidence) into simulated litigation negotiation, a different domain and research team.
findings.source_title: Psychological Barriers to Litigation Settlement: An Experimental Approach
